No,I read Montaigne who said self-revelation is the purpose of discourse, which, in his day, meant knowing whether to be flattered if a friend didn’t use a food-taster, or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping on an in-law. outputs.L1:
Sometimes, mystified by the behavior of one of my sons, my wife will point out whether it is age-appropriate, leaving me to wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on television and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son, with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. Yet I did not yell at the doctors who refused my insurance, nor grow angry with a friend who advised me to soak it in bourbon and garlic. No, instead I read Montaigne, who held that self-revelation is the very purpose of discourse—which, in his day, meant knowing whether to feel flattered when a friend dispensed with a food-taster, or amused when a witch cast a spell of weeping upon an in-law.

Blaise Monluc, the king's lieutenant general during the civil wars, Montaigne tells us, threw so many hanged Protestants down a well that one could reach in and touch the topmost head. Yes, Monluc—who was fond of declaring, "When the scaffolds are full, use trees"—knew precisely what was appropriate.

On occasion, I will duck into a lobby to avoid greeting a friend, not because my mind goes blank and I cannot recall his name, though that is true, but because I must flee what is darkest within me. In other words, when one is evicted from a strange lobby into a stranger street—where every scaffold is full and bodies dangle in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon, without context, explanation, or sympathy—it is good to know, even if only for a moment, how to live among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.

Yet I didn't scream at the physicians who turned down my insurance, nor did I lose my temper with a companion who suggested I steep it in a mixture of bourbon and garlic. Instead, I turned to Montaigne, who claimed that the point of conversation is to reveal oneself—which, back in his era, involved figuring out whether you should feel honored that a friend dined without a food-taster present, or entertained when a witch placed a curse of endless weeping upon a relative by marriage. According to Montaigne, Blaise Monluc, who served as the king's lieutenant general throughout the civil wars, hurled such a quantity of executed Protestants into a well that you could stretch your arm down and lay a hand on the skull of the uppermost corpse. Indeed, Monluc—who liked to declare, "When the scaffolds are full, use trees"—understood the meaning of appropriate. Now and then I'll dash into a lobby to sidestep having to greet an acquaintance, not because my thoughts evaporate and his name escapes me, though that does happen, but rather because I need to escape whatever is most shadowed within myself. Put differently, when I'm cast out of some unfamiliar lobby onto an even more unfamiliar street—where each scaffold is occupied and corpses sway in the deep blue melancholy of afternoon, stripped of any context, reason, or compassion—it helps to grasp, if only for an instant, how one ought to live among those who are relevant, those who are passionate, and those who are lost.

# Reflections on Behavior and Meaning

My wife has a way of putting things that stops me short. When she remarked on what was "age-appropriate" for our sons, I found myself turning the phrase over in my mind, applying it not to the boys but to myself. What, I wondered, was age-appropriate for me? Certainly not the spectacle I made shouting at ballplayers on the television screen—men who could neither hear me nor benefit from my advice, yet who somehow provoked in me a passion I could scarcely explain. There is something puzzling in these behaviors we adults permit ourselves, these small irrationalities we would never tolerate in our children.

This puzzlement deepened after my son injured his ankle with a wild pitch. One might expect a father to respond with anger, or at least with the sharp reflex of frustration. Instead, I found myself turning, almost involuntarily, to the philosophy of Montaigne. There was comfort there, and clarity, in the pages of a man who had spent his life examining the strange contradictions of human conduct.

Montaigne believed that the true purpose of discourse was not persuasion or instruction but self-revelation. To speak, to write, to argue—these were ultimately ways of disclosing oneself, of laying bare the contours of one's own mind. He illustrated this conviction through countless historical anecdotes, drawing on the social customs and behaviors of different peoples and eras, using the wider world as a mirror in which to examine his own nature.

Among these stories, I recall the one he tells of Blaise Monluc, the military commander who executed Protestants with a brutality that chills the reader even now. What struck Montaigne—and what struck me—was the cynicism with which Monluc justified himself, claiming to know precisely what was "appropriate" to the circumstances. That word again: appropriate. How easily it can serve as a mask for cruelty, how readily we invoke propriety to excuse the darkest of our impulses.

And here I must make my own confession. I have fled from friends, avoided their company, precisely to escape confronting the darkness within myself—the same darkness that, in its extreme form, Monluc dressed up as duty. What I am seeking, in Montaigne and elsewhere, is some understanding of how to live meaningfully amid the confusion and sorrow that seem inseparable from being human. It is not an easy search, and I cannot claim to have found its end. But perhaps the searching itself, the willingness to look inward rather than away, is where a meaningful life begins.

# On Knowing How to Live

My son broke his arm last Tuesday, though "broke" hardly captures the mundane absurdity of it. He was not climbing anything heroic, not testing the limits of his young body against some worthy obstacle. He simply tripped over the leg of a kitchen chair, fell in the most ordinary way imaginable, and landed wrong. There was the sickening angle of it, the trip to the hospital, the waiting, the cast. And there was, throughout, my own peculiar reaction—a mixture of tenderness and irritation that shamed me even as I felt it. I found myself annoyed with him, this small suffering person, for the disruption, for the way his pain rearranged my afternoon. What kind of father feels this? What kind of man?

I have been reading Montaigne again, which is perhaps why the question presents itself in this form. Montaigne, who made a whole book out of asking what kind of man he was, who turned the examination of his own inconsistencies into an art. He was not embarrassed to record that he had a poor memory, that he disliked certain foods, that his mind wandered during serious occasions. He gives us everything, or seems to—the essayist as a man turned inside out, willing to reveal what the rest of us conceal. And I wonder, sitting with my son's cast drying and my own small meanness still fresh, whether this is courage or merely a different sort of vanity.

The question of self-revelation troubles me. There is a fashion now for confession, for the display of one's wounds and failings as a kind of currency. But Montaigne's confessions were never quite that. He revealed himself not to be admired for his honesty but to arrive at some understanding of the human creature by way of the only specimen he could examine at length. "Each man bears the entire form of the human condition," he wrote. To know oneself was to know something general, something that might be useful. My irritation at my son's broken arm, then, is not merely my failing—it is data, evidence about what a man is.

But here is where the histories complicate matters. I have also been reading Blaise de Monluc, the sixteenth-century soldier whose memoirs Montaigne knew, a man who recorded his brutalities with the same candor Montaigne brought to his digestion. Monluc hanged men, burned villages, put populations to the sword, and he tells us so without apparent shame. He too is revealing himself. He too is offering the entire form of the human condition. And what it reveals is monstrous—the capacity of a man to do terrible things and to feel, apparently, that they were appropriate to his station, his age, his role. There is a chilling propriety in Monluc, a sense that this was simply what a man of his kind did at that moment in his life.

This is what unsettles me: the notion of age-appropriate behavior. We speak of it now regarding children—what a boy should be able to manage, what falls are ordinary for his years. But the phrase reaches further than we like to admit. Every age, every era, has its sense of what a man of a certain standing ought to do, and this sense can accommodate almost anything. Monluc knew how to conduct himself. He was never in doubt. He moved through his slaughters with the confidence of a man who understood his role completely. And I, who cannot even manage the correct emotion toward my injured child, look at that confidence with something close to envy and something close to horror.

For the difficulty is precisely this: how does one know how to conduct oneself? The brutal have their certainties. The confident have their scripts. But for those of us who feel the ground shifting, who suspect that our irritations and avoidances reveal us more truly than our virtues, the question remains open and painful. I think of the times I have crossed a street to avoid a conversation, ducked into a doorway to escape an acquaintance, pretended not to see someone I knew. These small evasions—what do they say about my capacity to live among others? Montaigne, too, describes his retreats, his preference for his tower and his books over the demands of society. But he made of his withdrawal a philosophy, while mine feels only like cowardice dressed up in the language of temperament.

Perhaps the honest position is to admit that we do not know how to live, that no one has ever fully known, that Monluc's terrible certainty and Montaigne's supple self-examination are two responses to the same fundamental ignorance. We are dropped into our lives without instruction, expected to conduct ourselves with wisdom we have not been given, among people—the relevant, the passionate, and the confused—whose own bewilderment we cannot fully see beneath their confident surfaces.

My son's arm will heal. In six weeks the cast comes off, and he will have forgotten the fall, though he may keep some faint wariness of kitchen chairs. He is learning, in his small way, how bodies move through the world and where they meet resistance. I am still learning too, more slowly, with less grace—not how to keep my body from harm but how to be a person among persons, how to feel the right things, how to reveal without vanity and withdraw without cowardice. Montaigne offers no final answer, and neither does Monluc, and neither, God knows, do I. There is only the ongoing attention, the willingness to look at oneself in the moment of failure and to ask, again, the old unanswerable question: how, among all these others, is one meant to live?

# On Reading Montaigne

**Sometimes** the oldest books feel the most alive. I discovered this truth quite by accident, pulling a worn volume from a shelf on a rainy afternoon when I had nothing better to do. It was the *Essays* of Michel de **Montaigne**, and what began as idle curiosity became one of the most rewarding literary companionships of my life.

Montaigne, writing in the sixteenth century, invented a form so intimate that reading him feels less like study and more like conversation. He wrote about everything—friendship, fear, thumbs, cannibals, the education of children, and above all, himself. "I am myself the matter of my book," he confessed, and in that honesty he became a mirror for readers across four hundred years.

What draws me back to him again and again is his refusal to pretend. **Sometimes** he contradicts himself from one page to the next, and rather than hide it, he embraces it. "If my mind could gain a firm footing," he admitted, "I would not make essays, I would make decisions." His genius lay in accepting that human beings are wandering, uncertain creatures, and that wisdom begins with admitting how little we truly know.

There is a particular passage I return to about death—not as something to dread, but as the natural conclusion of a life fully lived. He believed that the value of life lies not in its length but in its use. Some people, he noted, have lived long yet lived very little.

When I close his book at the **last** page, I never feel the sense of finality that other authors leave behind. Montaigne does not offer conclusions so much as an invitation to keep thinking, to keep questioning, and to keep discovering ourselves in his ancient, endlessly modern words.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem that blends personal, everyday moments—like a sports injury or avoiding a friend in a lobby—with reflections on Montaigne and historical violence during the French civil wars.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Cruelty

The physical therapist folds my knee toward my chest and asks if this hurts, and I say no when I mean yes, which is the same lie I tell when I duck behind the concrete pillar in the lobby to avoid Daniel, who once loaned me a book I never returned. Montaigne wrote his essays in a tower lined with a thousand volumes, retreating from a France where Catholics and Protestants unstitched each other in the streets, where a man might be pulled apart by horses for the crime of praying wrong.

I ice my knee for twenty minutes, no more, the sheet of instructions warns, as if excess care were its own injury. Montaigne could not bear to watch a chicken's neck wrung. He confessed this—that cruelty was the vice he most despised, more than the massacres piling up outside his window, he felt the small deaths, the hunted hare, the trapped bird. Meanwhile in Paris the bodies floated in the Seine so thick you could not see the water. Saint Bartholomew's Day. Thousands in a night. He does not describe it. He describes instead his own inability to lie, his memory's failures, the shape of his own kidney stones.

Daniel sees me anyway. He always does. He lifts his hand, and I lift mine, and we perform the choreography of men who owe each other something small and unpayable. How strange, Montaigne says across four centuries, that we are so tender to ourselves and so easy with the suffering of others. The knee will heal. The book is somewhere in a box I have not opened since I moved. There is a kind of violence in forgetting, and a kind of mercy, and Montaigne knew he could not tell them apart, and neither can I, standing in the lobby, my hand still raised, the wars still burning in the book I never gave back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person literary meditation on what it means to know "how to live," weaving together fatherhood, aging, Montaigne's essays, and dark historical anecdotes.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Knowing How to Live

My daughter asks me, from the backseat, whether I will die. She is four. The question arrives the way weather arrives—without apology, filling the whole sky of the car. *Someday,* I tell her, and watch in the mirror as she turns this over, then returns to her window, satisfied by an answer I find intolerable.

Montaigne wrote that to philosophize is to learn how to die, borrowing the line from Cicero, who borrowed it from the dying. But later—older, softer, having fallen from a horse and tasted the sweetness of his own near-oblivion—he changed his mind. *It is a thing of nothing,* he decided. Death would take care of itself; the body knew the way, as it knew how to digest, how to sleep. The harder art, the one requiring a lifetime, was knowing how to live. *Our great and glorious masterpiece is to live appropriately.*

I am forty-one. I have begun to feel the machinery.

---

There is a story I cannot stop returning to. When the plague came through Provence, whole villages dug their own graves in the fields and lay down in them to wait, so that no one healthy would have to handle the bodies. Montaigne records it. They *chose* their graves and lay there, looking up at the same indifferent sky my daughter studies from her car seat, and they died in the beds they had prepared, patient as seeds.

I used to read such things for the shudder. Now I read them for the instruction. Those people knew something. Not how to die—dying required nothing of them—but how to arrange their leaving so that it cost the living as little as possible. Their masterpiece was a kind of courtesy. To depart without becoming a burden. Is that not, in the end, a way of loving?

---

My own father is shrinking. This is not metaphor. The doorframes he once filled he now passes through with room to spare, and when I embrace him I feel the architecture beneath the flesh, the scaffolding showing through. He was a man of enormous certainties. He is becoming a man of questions, and the questions are gentler than the certainties ever were.

Watching him, I understand that I am watching a demonstration. He is teaching me the last thing, the way he taught me to shave, to drive, to hold a hammer near the head for control. He does not know he is teaching. That is what makes it teaching.

Montaigne buried five of his six children. He mentions this almost in passing—*I lost two or three children in infancy, not without regret, but without great sorrow*—and scholars have wrung their hands over the coldness of it for four hundred years. But I think I understand him now, or begin to. He is not cold. He is a man standing in the plague-field of his own century, and he has learned that to survive it he must ration his grief the way the starving ration bread. To feel everything fully would be to lie down in the grave beside them. He chose, instead, to live. The coldness is a discipline. The coldness is love that has decided to remain useful.

---

Here is another anecdote, and I offer it because the dark ones are the ones that teach. During the Terror, they guillotined so many that the ground beneath the scaffold grew saturated, and the smell reached the Tuileries, and even the executioners complained. But the condemned, we are told, developed customs. They held little academies in the prisons, rehearsing how to mount the steps with grace. They practiced the final walk. They gave lessons to each other in the one thing that remained wholly theirs: the manner of the ending.

I find this unbearable and I find it magnificent, and I no longer believe those are different feelings. To be stripped of everything—liberty, future, the faces of your children—and to salvage from the wreckage the single sovereign act of *how you carry yourself across the last ten meters*—this is the human thing. This is the masterpiece performed on the smallest possible stage.

---

So what does it mean, to know how to live?

I thought, when I was young, that it meant intensity. Burning. The full cup drained. I collected experiences the way my daughter collects the smooth stones she finds, certain that accumulation was the same as wealth.

Now I think it means something closer to *attention.* Montaigne, in his tower, reading his beloved classics with his motto carved into the beams—*Que sais-je?*, what do I know?—was not accumulating. He was attending. He watched himself think. He watched his own mind change and did not scold it for changing. *I do not portray being,* he wrote. *I portray passing.* He understood that a life is not a monument but a river, and that to live well is not to dam it but to know its water intimately as it goes.

My daughter is passing. This afternoon she is four; by the time I finish this thought she will be someone I have to reintroduce myself to. My father is passing, into that gentleness. I am passing—the machinery reminds me hourly. Everything I love is water, and I have been trying my whole life to hold it in my hands, and the great secret that Montaigne kept trying to tell me, that the plague-villagers knew, that the condemned rehearsed in their cells, is this:

You do not learn how to live in order to escape the passing. You learn how to live *by attending to it.* By pressing your palm flat against the river and feeling it move. By answering *someday* honestly to the child, and then—this is the whole art—by turning, as she does, back to the window, back to the light coming through it, back to the ordinary miracle of the next unhurried mile.

She has fallen asleep now, in the mirror. Her mouth is open. She trusts the car to carry her, trusts me to steer, trusts the world to still be there when she wakes.

That trust is the thing I am trying to deserve. That deserving is what it means to know how to live.

*Que sais-je?* Only this. Only the road, only the sleeping child, only the diminishing father, only the field where the patient dead lay down and looked up at the sky and let go—teaching us, across the centuries, the one lesson we resist to the last:

that it is all, always, passing, and that this is not the tragedy.

This is the invitation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemplative essay-poem in the style of a contemporary poet, moving associatively from a wife's observations about parenting to reading Montaigne to Blaise Monluc's atrocities and back to a moment of personal shame.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Government of Children

My wife says the trouble with our discipline
is that we mean it only half the time.
The child knows this. The child is a barometer
for our conviction, reads the pressure
of our wanting-to-be-loved against
our wanting-to-be-obeyed, and finds us
wanting. *You have to choose,* she says,
scraping the plates. *You can't do both.*

And I think of Montaigne in his tower,
the beams inscribed with sentences
he'd measured himself against for years,
writing that he had never once
been able to watch a child punished
without it wounding something in him—
that he preferred, he said, the way
we govern children by pure reason,
if such a thing were possible,
though he admitted it was not,
that force was always somewhere in the room,
a dog we keep chained just outside the door
and pretend we cannot hear.

*

He tells the story—or I've placed it
next to his, the way you set two stones
on a sill and let the light decide
their kinship—of Blaise de Monluc,
Marshal of France, who in his memoirs
confessed with a soldier's arithmetic
how many he had hanged, how many towns
he'd emptied into their own wells,
believing terror was a kind of mercy,
that one village burned would spare him ten.
He wrote it down. That's the thing
that stops me. He sat, as I sit now,
and gave an accounting, and slept.
And on the last page, old, he grieved—
not for the burned, but for a son
he'd raised so sternly, kept at such
a formal distance of respect,
that the boy died having never known
his father loved him. *I lost him twice,*
Monluc wrote, *once to the sea,
and once, before that, to my own
cold manner of loving.* The man
who fed the wells his enemies
wept only for the one he'd starved
of tenderness, his own.

*

And here the essay wants to close
its hand around a lesson,
the way I want to close mine
around the child's small wrist
and *make* the moment obey—

*

I hit him once. Not hard.
A palm against the back of a leg.
He was three. He'd run toward the road.
That's the story I tell, and it's true,
but the truth beneath the true
is that I was ashamed of him
in front of strangers, that my hand
moved from embarrassment
before it moved from fear,
that I dressed the one in the other's coat
and have kept it dressed for years.

He doesn't remember. I do.
This is the whole of it: the ones
we harm forget, and we
become the wells we filled,
carrying the small dark water
of it down inside us, brackish,
tasting each time we bend
to drink from our own kindness
the mineral of what we are.

*

My wife is right. You have to choose.
But Montaigne, closing his book,
would say the self is not a thing
that chooses once and stands.
It chooses hourly, badly, and revises,
and the tower is only a room
where a man agrees to watch himself
without the mercy of a verdict.

The child is asleep now.
I go in, as I do each night,
to put the blanket back
across the leg I struck
in a year he cannot reach,
and I stand there in the almost-dark
governing nothing,
loved for reasons I did not earn
and cannot, being what I am,
entirely believe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of literary nonfiction that uses Montaigne's idea that "self-revelation is the purpose of discourse" as a thematic anchor, incorporating humor, an ankle injury, and imagery of hanged bodies and empty scaffolds.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of an Ankle

Montaigne believed that the purpose of discourse was self-revelation—that in speaking, in the endless clarification of what we think, we perform the strange archaeology of digging ourselves up. I did not know this when I fell off the curb outside the pharmacy, but I know it now, having spent six weeks with my foot elevated on three pillows and nothing to do but talk to myself about the nature of talking to myself.

The fall was undignified in the specific way that all self-inflicted injuries are undignified. There was no adversary, no dramatic ice, no villain. There was only me, a curb of ordinary height, and the sudden treachery of my own ankle folding like a bad hand of cards. The sound it made—a wet, private *pop*—was the sound of my body confessing something to me that I had not asked about.

I want to tell you it hurt. It did. But what interests me, in the Montaignean sense, is that my first response was not pain but *narration*. Before I had even hit the pavement I was already composing the story of the fall, already deciding how I would tell it, already rehearsing the self-deprecating shrug. *You won't believe what I did.* We are, all of us, sportscasters of our own humiliation, and the color commentary begins before the play is over.

---

Here is a thing you learn when you cannot walk: the house fills up with images of stillness. I lay on the couch and stared at the coat rack in the hall, from which hung my jackets in a row—shoulders slumped, sleeves dangling, the whole assembly swaying faintly when the heat kicked on. And I thought, with the morbid clarity that painkillers grant: *hanged men*. A gallows of outerwear. Three coats swinging gently in the domestic breeze, executed for crimes I could not name.

This is what the mind does when the body is stilled. It reaches for the extreme. Montaigne wrote constantly of death—kept it in his pocket like a coin, turned it over, examined the King's face on it. He believed that to philosophize was to learn how to die, and I believe that to be laid up with a bad ankle is to be given a small, ridiculous rehearsal of the larger stillness. You lie there. You cannot flee. You are, for the first time in weeks, *available* to yourself.

And what I found, when I became available, was not profundity. It was inventory.

---

The empty scaffold is more frightening than the occupied one. This I decided on day nine.

A body hanging is a fact, terrible but complete—a sentence that has ended. But the empty scaffold is *anticipation*. It is the machinery of consequence with the consequence still pending. It says: *someone will hang here, and it might be you, and we are ready whenever you are.* I thought of this because I had a follow-up appointment with the orthopedist, and the X-ray light-box in his office—glowing, empty, waiting for the film of my own interior architecture—struck me as its own kind of scaffold. The place where the verdict gets hung up for viewing.

"It's a sprain," the doctor said, "not a fracture." And I felt the peculiar disappointment of the acquitted. Some part of me had wanted the drama of a break. A sprain is the injury of the clumsy; a fracture is the injury of the *unlucky*, and we would all so much rather be unlucky than clumsy. To be unlucky is to have been chosen. To be clumsy is merely to have been *yourself*, too hard, at the wrong moment.

There it is again. Self-revelation, arriving uninvited, tracking mud across the clean floor of my self-image.

---

Montaigne's genius was that he refused to pretend he was better than he was. He told you about his kidney stones. He told you about his failing memory, his preference for certain wines, the exact and humbling operations of his bowels. He understood that the essay—the *attempt*—was not a performance of wisdom but an excavation of a single, particular, flawed man, on the theory that the particular is the only road to the universal we have.

So let me be particular. Here is what six weeks of enforced stillness revealed, in the honest ledger:

That I define myself almost entirely by motion, by the ability to leave a room. That when I could not leave rooms, I discovered how much of my identity had been *fleeing*. That I am kinder to strangers than to the people who bring me tea. That I had been using my busyness the way the empty scaffold uses its rope—as a threat held over my own head, a way of insisting on my seriousness, my consequence, my *deserving* of exhaustion.

The ankle took all that away. It hung my busyness up by the neck until it stopped kicking. And in the silence that followed, I heard myself think, and thinking, I met the man doing the thinking, and he was—it must be said—somewhat ridiculous. A person who had mistaken velocity for virtue. Who fell off a curb because he was, as always, hurrying toward something he would not have wanted once he arrived.

---

I am walking again now, with a slight and shameful limp that I am tempted to exaggerate for sympathy. (This too is self-revelation: I have learned I would trade a great deal of honesty for a small amount of pity.) The coats hang in the hall, and they are only coats again—the executed have been pardoned, or perhaps I have simply stopped seeing the noose in everything, which is what recovery is.

But I keep with me the thing the stillness taught me, the thing Montaigne knew: that we do not speak in order to inform. We speak in order to find out who is speaking. Every sentence is a small scaffold on which we hang a version of ourselves to see whether it will hold. Most of them don't. Most of them kick and struggle and reveal, in their dying, that the self we meant to present was a fraud, and the true self is the one caught watching, embarrassed, taking notes.

I fell off a curb. I told you about it. And in the telling—here is the whole secret, the entire estate of Montaigne compressed into one throbbing joint—I have introduced myself to you and, more strangely, to me.

The purpose of discourse is self-revelation. The ankle merely made me sit still long enough to be revealed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness meditation about fleeing "what is darkest in me," connecting domestic life, historical cruelty, and the search for how to live among "the relevant, the passionate, and the confused."
counterfactuals.output:
# What Is Darkest

I am running again, always running, from the kitchen where the kettle sings its small domestic hymn, from the table set for two, the folded napkins, the ordinary grace of Tuesday—running not toward but away, away from what is darkest in me, the thing that wakes before I wake and dresses in my clothes.

How ordinary the surface. How the milk goes sour in its carton. How I stack the plates and think of nothing, think of everything, think of the men who stacked the bodies, who went home after and washed their hands and ate the bread their wives had baked. This is the terror—not that they were monsters but that they were like this, were like me, folding napkins.

*What is darkest in me* wears a familiar face.

I cannot outrun it through the rooms of this house, the hallway lined with photographs, the children sleeping, the tenderness that is real, that is *so real*, and yet—and yet the same hand that strokes the hair could sign the order, could look away, could choose the comfortable silence over the difficult word. History is not behind us. It sleeps in the walls. It waits in the soft machinery of the self that says: *not my concern, not now, not here.*

So I am learning, slowly, how to live—

among the relevant, who will not let me sleep,
among the passionate, who burn and burn and shame my lukewarm heart,
among the confused, my truest kin, who do not know, who cannot know, who stumble through the ash of what came before us asking only: *how then? how now? how do we hold the knife and the bread in the same two hands?*

There is no fleeing. There is only turning. Turning to face the darkest room, opening the door, saying: *I see you. You are mine. I will not let you dress in my clothes today.*

The kettle sings. The napkins wait.
I set the table for the ones who are still coming.
